 UFC’s Brian Ortega eager to show growth through changes 
 The South Bay fighter, in a new weight class and with a new fight team, takes on Dan Hooker at UFC Fight Night 294

 The South Bay’s Brian Ortega will square off with New Zealand lightweight Dan Hooker on the UFC Fight Night 294 main card on Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026, in Doha, Qatar. (Photo by Hans Gutknecht, Los Angeles Daily News/SCNG)
 By Brian Martin | bmartin@scng.com PUBLISHED: November 19, 2026 at 2:49 PM PST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... New weight class. New fight team. New addition to the family.
 Put them all together and it’s easy to see why the South Bay’s Brian Ortega has a new outlook.
 “This time, I just had freedom to train and eat and relax and smile and bond, and it was physical and mental actually,” Ortega said via a Zoom call this week from Doha, Qatar. “You know, it was good.”
 After years of struggles on the scale, the UFC star has moved to a new division, which he will test Saturday in Qatar when he faces fellow fight veteran Dan Hooker on the UFC Fight Night 294 main card.
 Ortega, 35, has finally made the move from featherweight to lightweight, finding life better at 155 pounds versus 145 pounds. Hooker (24-15) has bounced between the divisions as well. The New Zealander has lost three in a row – two via TKO and one via an arm-triangle submission – ahead of what Ortega calls “the battle of old men.”
 “I think we’re both at the same place, you know, where we’ve had wars. We fought the best of the best. I think our prime days are obviously behind us,” the Lomita resident said of his 36-year-old opponent. “But this is a battle where you actually genuinely see two people who don’t give a ‘you know what’ and they show up to fight. I think he’s like, ‘Hey, I’m gonna show up, I’m gonna fight, I’m gonna bang it out.’ I’m over here like, ‘Yo, I’m gonna show up and I’m gonna fight and I’m gonna win.’”
 ‘I was in fat camp’
 Having twice come up short for the featherweight title, the lifelong 145-pounder is happily settling in at lightweight for the first time. Weight cuts have tested Ortega (16-5, 1 NC) many times, even coming close to having his long locks hacked off so he could make weight before UFC 214 at Honda Center.
 Sometimes the weight cuts went seamlessly. Other times, his toughest opponent was his own body as he pushed himself to shed the last few pounds.
 “I think the dope part was, train hard, and instead of coming back after training and having a small portion of food, I was able to have good amounts, good-sized portions to eat, and for the first time in my life, that was a possibility,” he said.
 “You know, I wasn’t in fat camp. Let’s just be honest, bro. Everything was just like I was in fat camp.”
 The move up in weight was largely spurred by Ortega’s last fight 15 months ago in Shanghai against former bantamweight champion Aljamain Sterling.
 Then again, passing out for 30 minutes and waking up in a hospital in China, hooked up to IVs and wires and surrounded by loved ones, will do that.
 “Close to death, and a lot of people don’t understand that,” Ortega said.
 It is a delicate dance nearly every fighter endures. Shed several pounds the week of the fight, including many the night before, all in the name of barely hitting the mark and then packing it back on in the ensuing 24 hours for the fight.
 The process left Ortega a shell of himself – and not for the first time.
 “Mentally, I wasn’t there. And then physically, I’m drained,” Ortega said. “And then by the time you gotta fight, you’re just, you been out of whack for a while, so you don’t have that same push and that same drive and that same … you know, you’re just not on fire anymore.”
 Ortega still fought in Shanghai, albeit at a catchweight of 153 pounds and looking spent. He lost via unanimous decision, lasting all five rounds.
 New environment
 “Bro, it’s dope. It’s something that I believe should have happened a long time ago.”
 That’s Ortega’s reaction when asked about his recent move to Team Body Shop, training with PFL star A.J. McKee and under the expertise of his father Antonio McKee.
 The drive alone, eschewing Huntington Beach for Metroflex in Hawaiian Gardens, is appealing. But what Ortega found with the McKees is a kinship and guidance he’s been sorely missing.
 “It’s amazing. I developed a bond, you know? And it’s cool. I’ve had heartbreaks in this game,” said Ortega, who has gone through a few trainers. “Finding someone who cares about you, whether the outcome is what you wanted or not. To have someone genuinely just show love. It’s hard, man. I found it.”
 In addition to the emotional support, Ortega values what the McKees have brought to his game. The father and son carry dozens of years of experience in the fight game, with Antonio’s leadership and A.J.’s immense talent.
 And A.J. appreciates how much he and Ortega complement each other.
 “He’s showing me how to pull stuff from different angles, and I’m showing him how to not focus on jiu-jitsu and how to cause damage and make them fall into the submission,” A.J. McKee said. “So he’s growing, man. This guy, he’s been doing so much on his own for so long and it’s awesome, dude. I think give him a year from now and the growth that we’re gonna see out of Ortega, it’s gonna be Brian 2.0.”
 New life
 Ortega was scheduled to fight in his hometown of Los Angeles at UFC 331 on Sept. 19, but a cut over his eye while training forced him out of his bout against Renato Moicano.
 It might have been all for the best. About a month before the fight, his wife, Stephanie, gave birth to their third son.
 And Ortega is positively smitten.
 “He’s amazing. Being a dad for maybe the third and final time – who knows? – but it feels amazing, man. I have this beautiful boy that I’ve been blessed with, and that kid is such a gift,” Ortega said. “Literally this whole trip, I’m over here just watching videos of him. I miss him already, man. And I’m not the sappy type, but that little guy got me.”
 For so many changes in his life, Ortega has encountered newfound comfort. And in feeling physically healthier, it has synced up with better mental health and emotional state of peace.
 Ortega says he feels like he’s home.
 “I actually get to be me,” he said. “That’s just the closest thing I can say. I get to be me.”
 UFC FIGHT NIGHT 294
 When: Saturday
 Where: ABHA Arena, Doha, Qatar
 How to watch: Paramount+ (prelims, 4 a.m. PT; main card, 7 a.m. PT)
